      3986 -## Part 8 — Resilience: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers, 
           -Scalability                                                  
      3987 -                                                             
      3988 -### Timeout Budgets                                          
      3989 -                                                             
      3990 -Every external call is wrapped with `asyncio.wait_for`. `Data
           -Requirement.timeout_ms` overrides the                        
      3991 -default per fetch. Overall per-turn target for Tier 3a: ≤ 1.5
           -s to first LLM chunk.                                        
      3992 -                                                             
      3993 -| Call | Hard Timeout | Notes |                              
      3994 -|---|---|---|                                                
      3995 -| Haiku SLM (classification) | 2,000ms | Fail fast; SLM fallb
           -ack fires (see below) |                                      
      3996 -| Khoj `searchProperties` | 1,500ms | User-blocking; fast-fai
           -l over waiting |                                             
      3997 -| Casa `getPropertyDetail` | 2,000ms | |                     
      3998 -| Venus `getFloorPlans` / `getBrochure` | 2,000ms | |        
      3999 -| Gandalf `getPriceTrends` | 2,000ms | |                     
      4000 -| Odin `getLocalityDetail` / `getRatingsReviews` | 2,000ms | 
           -|                                                            
      4001 -| Autosuggest `resolveEntity` | 500ms | Hot-path entity resol
           -ution; skip on timeout |                                     
      4002 -| Claude stream (time-to-first-token) | 5,000ms | Abort strea
           -m if no chunk within 5s |                                    
      4003 -| Redis read (cache / session load) | 50ms | Fail open — trea
           -t as cache miss, never block |                               
      4004 -| Redis write (session save) | 100ms | Log + continue; handle
           -d by optimistic locking |                                    
      4005 -| Kafka publish | 500ms | Queued locally on failure; see reli
           -ability below |                                              
      4006 -                                                             
      4007 -```python                                                    
      4008 -# TOOL_DEFAULT_TIMEOUTS — used by execute_prefetch when DataR
           -equirement.timeout_ms is absent                              
      4009 -# Values in milliseconds; converted to seconds via / 1000 whe
           -n passed to asyncio.wait_for.                                
      4010 -TOOL_DEFAULT_TIMEOUTS: dict[str, int] = {                    
      4011 -    'searchProperties':       1500,                          
      4012 -    'resolveEntity':           500,

      4041 -                                                             
      4042 -### Retry Policy                                             
      4043 -                                                             
      4044 -Retries are allowed only for idempotent reads against transie
           -nt errors.                                                   
      4045 -Write-side tools (`contactSeller`, `shortlistProperty`) must 
           -**never** be retried automatically.                          
      4046 -                                                             
      4047 -| Error | Retryable? | Strategy |                            
      4048 -|---|---|---|                                                
      4049 -| 5xx (500, 502, 503, 504) | Yes — reads only | 1 retry after
           - 300ms |                                                     
      4050 -| Network timeout | Yes — reads only | 1 retry immediately | 
      4051 -| 429 with `Retry-After` | Yes | Wait header value; max 1 ret
           -ry |                                                         
      4052 -| 400 Bad Request | No | Bad params; retrying won't help |   
      4053 -| 404 Not Found | No | Entity does not exist |               
      4054 -| 401 / 403 | No | Auth failure; surface to user |           
      4055 -| Write-side tools | Never | Duplicate side effects (double l
           -ead, double shortlist) |                                     
      4056 -                                                             
      4057 -Max retries: **1**. No multi-hop backoff loops — the per-turn
           - latency budget cannot absorb them.                          
      4058 -Retry logic lives in the `CachedExecutorPort` implementation,
           - using `tenacity` (`@retry`, `wait_fixed`, `stop_after_attemp
           -t`) — not in graph nodes.                                    
      4059 -                                                             
      4060 -### SLM Failure Fallback                                     
      4061 -                                                             
      4062 -If SLM classification fails (timeout or 5xx) after 1 retry:  
      4063 -- Route to `out_of_scope` Tier 0 handler                     
      4064 -- Emit canned response: *"I'm having trouble understanding th
           -at — could you rephrase?"*                                   
      4065 -- Log `classifier_unavailable` metric; alert if rate > 1% ove
           -r 5 minutes                                                  
      4066 -                                                             
      4067 -Do not attempt to classify with a backup model — the graph is
           - already behind budget.                                      
      4068 -                                                             
      4069 -### Circuit Breakers                                         
      4070 -                                                             
      4071 -A circuit breaker wraps each backend via the `ToolExecutorPor
           -t` implementation.                                           
      4072 -Prevents cascading failures when a backend is degraded — fail
           - fast instead of queue-and-wait.                             
      4073 -                                                             
      4074 -```                                                          
      4075 -CLOSED (normal)                                              
      4076 -  → opens after 5 consecutive failures within 30s            
      4077 -OPEN (failing fast)                                          
      4078 -  → immediately rejects with CircuitOpenError for a cool-down
           - window                                                      
      4079 -  → fetch_data_node records this as a fetch_error (same path 
           -as timeout)                                                  
      4080 -HALF_OPEN                                                    
      4081 -  → allows 1 probe request after cool-down                   
      4082 -  → success → CLOSED; failure → OPEN again                   
      4083 -```                                                          
      4084 -                                                             
      4085 -| Backend | Open threshold | Cool-down |                     
      4086 -|---|---|---|                                                
      4087 -| Khoj | 5 failures | 15s |                                  
      4088 -| Casa | 5 failures | 15s |                                  
      4089 -| Venus / Gandalf / Odin | 5 failures | 15s |                
      4090 -| Autosuggest | 5 failures | 10s |                           
      4091 -| SLM (Haiku) | 3 failures | 30s |                           
      4092 -| Claude (LLM) | 3 failures | 30s |                          
      4093 -                                                             
      4094 -When a circuit is OPEN, the LLM is instructed via the `fetch_
           -errors` context block:                                       
      4095 -*"Data for [tool] is temporarily unavailable. Acknowledge thi
           -s and respond with what you have."*                          
      4096 -                                                             
      4097 -### Scalability Notes                                        
      4098 -                                                             
      4099 -**SSE and load balancing:**                                  
      4100 -SSE streaming requires the same instance to hold the in-fligh
           -t Claude stream for the duration of                          
      4101 -the response. Two options:                                   
      4102 -- **Option A (v1):** Sticky sessions at the load balancer key
           -ed by `session_id`. Simple; less                             
      4103 -  fault-tolerant if an instance goes down mid-stream.        
      4104 -- **Option B (multi-region):** Each instance publishes chunks
           - to a Redis Stream keyed by                                  
      4105 -  `session_id`; a thin edge layer subscribes and forwards to 
           -the client's SSE connection.                                 
      4106 -  Fully stateless instances; more complex.                   
      4107 -                                                             
      4108 -Recommendation: Option A for v1.                             
      4109 -                                                             
      4110 -**Session write conflicts:**                                 
      4111 -`SessionStorePort.save` uses an optimistic version field. If 
           -two concurrent turns on the same                             
      4112 -session attempt to write simultaneously, the second write ret
           -urns `false`. The caller                                     
      4113 -(`reconcileSessionConflict`) re-fetches session state and re-
           -applies only the safe fields                                 
      4114 -(turn list append, viewed property IDs). The session is never
           - left in a corrupted state.                                  
      4115 -                                                             
      4116 -**Kafka reliability:**                                       
      4117 -`persistToKafka` is not fire-and-forget. On publish failure, 
           -the message is placed in a local                             
      4118 -in-memory retry queue (ring buffer, max 500 entries). A backg
           -round worker retries every 5s for up                         
      4119 -to 10 minutes. After 10 minutes, the message is written to a 
           -dead-letter file and an alert fires.                         
      4120 -Messages are never silently dropped.                         
      4121 -                                                             
      4122 -**Cache stampede prevention:**                               
      4123 -When a cache miss occurs for a high-traffic key, a single-fli
           -ght lock ensures only one request                            
      4124 -calls the upstream API; all concurrent requests for the same 
           -key await that one in-flight promise.                        
      4125 -Cache TTLs are jittered ±10% to stagger expiry across hot key
           -s.                                                           
      4126 -                                                             
      4127 ----                                                          
      4128 -

      4608 -## Part 11 — Unified Platform Integration Contracts          
      4609 -                                                             
      4610 -This section documents how the Search & Discovery service plu
           -gs into the unified platform                                 
      4611 -gateway defined in `unified-platform-architecture.md`. It cov
           -ers authentication, handoff

      4616 -                                                             
      4617 -### 1. Session Token Validation                              
      4618 -                                                             
      4619 -The routing gateway issues a short-lived `session_token` when
           - it assigns a session to this                                
      4620 -service. Every subsequent request from the client must includ
           -e that token. The service                                    
      4621 -validates the token on each turn before loading session state
           -.                                                            
      4622 -                                                             
      4623 -#### Updated `ChatEventFromUser`                             
      4624 -                                                             
      4625 -```python                                                    
      4626 -class ChatEventFromUser(BaseModel):                          
      4627 -    # Existing fields (unchanged):                           
      4628 -    conversation_id: str           # derived from validated t
           -oken — not trusted from body                                 
      4629 -    message_type:    str           # 'text' | 'user_action' |
           - 'context' | 'system_event'                                  
      4630 -    content:         MessageContent                          
      4631 -                                                             
      4632 -    # New field — required for platform integration:         
      4633 -    session_token:   str           # gateway-issued JWT or op
           -aque token                                                   
      4634 -```                                                          
      4635 -                                                             
      4636 -> **Note:** `conversation_id` is included in the body for bac
           -kwards-compatibility with                                    
      4637 -> direct service calls (testing, admin tools) but is **not tr
           -usted** when a                                               
      4638 -> `session_token` is present. The authoritative `conversation
           -_id` is derived from the                                     
      4639 -> validated token.                                           
      4640 -                                                             
      4641 -#### Validation flow                                         
      4642 -                                                             
      4643 -```python                                                    
      4644 -async def resolve_session(body: ChatEventFromUser, request: R
           -equest) -> SessionState:                                     
      4645 -    """                                                      
      4646 -    1. Validate session_token — JWT verify (signature + exp) 
           -or Redis lookup                                              
      4647 -       mapping  session_token → conversation_id  (gateway wri
           -tes this on RouteResponse).                                  
      4648 -    2. Derive conversation_id from the token; ignore body.con
           -versation_id.                                                
      4649 -    3. Load session via session_store.load_by_conversation(co
           -nversation_id, request).                                     
      4650 -    4. Raise HTTP 401 if token is missing, signature invalid,
           - or expired.                                                 
      4651 -    """                                                      
      4652 -```                                                          
      4653 -                                                             
      4654 -| Validation outcome | HTTP response |                       
        40 +| Doc | Content |                                            
        41  |---|---|
      4656 -| Token valid, session found | 200 — proceed |               
      4657 -| Token signature invalid | 401 `{ "error": "invalid_token" }
           -` |                                                          
      4658 -| Token expired | 401 `{ "error": "token_expired" }` |       
      4659 -| Token valid, session not found | 404 `{ "error": "session_n
           -ot_found" }` |                                               
        42 +| [Model Registry](models/model-registry.md) | MODEL_REGISTRY
           +, ModelAssignment, provider adapters |                       
        43 +| [A/B Experiments](models/ab-experiments.md) | ExperimentCon
           +fig, success metrics, graduation |                           
        44

      5003 -### 7. Session Lifecycle                                     
      5004 -                                                             
      5005 -The SSE model is **one new connection per turn** — stateless 
           -at the transport layer:                                      
      5006 -                                                             
      5007 -```                                                          
      5008 -POST /chat/message  { session_token, content }   ← client sub
           -mits user message                                            
      5009 -GET  /chat/stream   { session_token }             ← client op
           -ens fresh SSE to receive response                            
      5010 -```                                                          
      5011 -                                                             
      5012 -The SSE stream opens, the pipeline runs, the service streams 
           -the response, and the HTTP response closes naturally after th
           -e final `chat_event { sourceMessageState: "COMPLETED" }`. Con
           -versation state lives in Redis / Postgres — not on the connec
           -tion.                                                        
      5013 -                                                             
      5014 -```                                                          
      5015 -connection_ack                        ← stream opened        
      5016 -message_delta × N                     ← LLM streaming (if app
           -licable)                                                     
      5017 -chat_event { COMPLETED }              ← end of response; HTTP
           - response closes                                             
      5018 -                                         FE detects COMPLETED
           - and re-enables input                                        
      5019 -```                                                          
      5020 -                                                             
      5021 -For the **next user message**, the client sends a new POST an
           -d opens a new GET /chat/stream. Any backend instance can hand
           -le it — no sticky sessions, no long-lived socket to maintain.
      5022 -                                                             
      5023 -**Session end (mode switch / timeout):** The gateway stops is
           -suing RouteResponses for this service. The service writes `Se
           -ssionRecord.ended_at` to the Registry when `session_token` is
           - no longer valid. No special SSE event is needed — the next P
           -OST simply returns 401 or is not made at all (client queries 
           -the gateway first).

      5029 -### Finding a Turn in LangSmith                              
      5030 -                                                             
      5031 -Every graph invocation creates a LangSmith run with `run_id =
           - request_id`. To find a specific bad turn:                   
      5032 -                                                             
      5033 -```bash                                                      
      5034 -# Python SDK                                                 
      5035 -from langsmith import Client                                 
      5036 -client = Client()                                            
      5037 -run = client.read_run(run_id='<request_id>')   # full tree: e
           -very node as a child run                                     
      5038 -```                                                          
      5039 -                                                             
      5040 -The LangSmith trace shows:                                   
      5041 -- Input and output for each graph node                       
      5042 -- Per-node wall-clock latency                                
      5043 -- Full LLM prompts and responses (system prompt + messages + 
           -tool definitions)                                            
      5044 -- Tool calls and their results                               
      5045 -                                                             
      5046 -Every log line emitted during that turn also carries `request
           -_id`, so structured log search returns                       
      5047 -the complete picture: which nodes ran, which fetches failed, 
           -what the SLM classified, what the LLM generated.

      5062 -    sanitize → derive → clarify → resolve_entities → route → 
           -summary → experiment →                                       
      5063 -    fetch_data → build_prompt. Stops before llm_node. No LLM

           -ctly what Claude would see.

      5068 -    return {                                                 
      5069 -        'system_prompt':        state['system_prompt'],

           -|

           -iant`; optional for `prompt_variant` |

      5471 -3. Set `enabled: false` + `end_date` on ExperimentConfig in `
           -experiments.yaml`

           -mple size) if any guardrail exceeds 3× its `max_delta` thresh

      5829 -#### Calibrated comparison logic                             
      5830 -                                                             
      5831 -```python                                                    
      5832 -@dataclass                                                   
      5833 -class SoftField:                                             
      5834 -    field:   str    # dot-notation path into output dict     
      5835 -    compare: Literal['exact', 'within_10pct', 'entity_match',
           - 'subset', 'key_presence']                                   
      5836 -    # exact:         field value == expected value exactly   
      5837 -    # within_10pct:  abs(actual - expected) / expected <= 0.1
           -0                                                            
      5838 -    # entity_match:  actual entity name is a substring of exp
           -ected or vice versa                                          
      5839 -    #                ("Andheri West" matches "Andheri"; "andh
           -eri" matches "Andheri West")                                 
      5840 -    # subset:        every element of expected appears in act
           -ual (list fields, e.g. bhk)                                  
      5841 -    # key_presence:  filter_delta contains at least the expec
           -ted keys (values not checked)                                
      5842 -                                                             
      5843 -def evaluate_case(actual: dict, expected: dict, calibration: 
           -CaseCalibration) -> CaseResult:                              
      5844 -    failures = []                                            
      5845 -                                                             
      5846 -    # Strict fields — exact match required                   
      5847 -    for field in calibration.strict_fields:                  
      5848 -        act = get_nested(actual, field)                      
      5849 -        exp = get_nested(expected, field)                    
      5850 -        if act != exp:                                       
      5851 -            failures.append(f'STRICT {field}: got {act!r}, ex
           -pected {exp!r}')                                             
      5852 -                                                             
      5853 -    # Soft fields — calibrated comparison                    
      5854 -    for soft in calibration.soft_fields:                     
      5855 -        act = get_nested(actual, soft.field)

           -lassification, LLM response, conversation summarisation) refe
           -rences a single MODEL_REGISTRY. Swapping a model is a config

           - adapter backs each Protocol at startup. The pipeline is unaw
           -are of which provider or model version is running.

        31 -## Part A — API Endpoints                                    
        32 -                                                             
        33 -### A1. Get Conversation ID                                  
        34 -                                                             
        35 -```                                                          
        36 -GET /api/v1/chat/get-conversation-id                         
        37 -Headers: login-auth-token (optional), token_id (optional)    
        38 -```                                                          
        39 -                                                             
        40 -Response:                                                    
        41 -```json                                                      
        42 -{                                                            
        43 -  "statusCode": "2XX",                                       
        44 -  "responseCode": "SUCCESS",                                 
        45 -  "data": {                                                  
        46 -    "conversationId": "string",                              
        47 -    "isNew": true                                            
        48 -  }                                                          
        49 -}                                                            
        50 -```                                                          
        51 -                                                             
        52 -**Backend behavior:**                                        
        53 -- If `login-auth-token` header is present → look up or create
           - a conversation for that user.                               
        54 -- If anonymous (`token_id` cookie present) → return the exist
           -ing conversation for that `tokenId`.                         
        55 -- If no tokens → create a new conversation, return `isNew: tr
           -ue`.                                                         
        56 -- `conversationId` = `session_id` in our session store.      
        57 -                                                             
        58 ----                                                          
        59 -                                                             
        60 -### A2. Get Conversation Details (History)                   
        61 -                                                             
        62 -```                                                          
        63 -GET /api/v1/chat/get-conversation-details                    
        64 -Headers: login-auth-token (optional), token_id               
        65 -Query params:                                                
        66 -  pageSize?:       number   (default 20)                     
        67 -  messagesAfter?:  string   (messageId cursor — mutually excl
           -usive with messagesBefore)                                   
        68 -  messagesBefore?: string   (messageId cursor)               
        69 -```                                                          
        70 -                                                             
        71 -Response:                                                    
        72 -```json                                                      
        73 -{                                                            
        74 -  "statusCode": "2XX",                                       
        75 -  "responseCode": "SUCCESS",                                 
        76 -  "data": {                                                  
        77 -    "conversationId": "string",                              
        78 -    "tokenId": "string",                                     
        79 -    "messages": [ /* ChatEventToUser[] — see Part B */ ],    
        80 -    "hasMore": true                                          
        81 -  }                                                          
        82 -}                                                            
        83 -```                                                          
        84 -                                                             
        85 -**Backend behavior:**                                        
        86 -- Returns persisted `ChatEventToUser` rows from the conversat
           -ion, sorted oldest-first within a page.                      
        87 -- `messagesAfter` and `messagesBefore` are exclusive cursors 
           -(not inclusive).                                             
        88 -- `tokenId` in the response is the anonymous session token — 
           -frontend persists it in the `houzy_token` cookie.            
        89 -- Messages include all types: `text`, `markdown`, `template`,
           - `user_action`.                                              
        90 -                                                             
        91 ----                                                          
        92 -                                                             
        93 -### A3. Send Message (Streaming — Primary Path)              
        94 -                                                             
        95 -```                                                          
        96 -POST /api/v1/chat/send-message-streamed?streamingEnabled=true
        97 -Headers:                                                     
        98 -  Content-Type: application/json                             
        99 -  Accept: text/event-stream                                  
       100 -  login-auth-token (optional)                                
       101 -Query params:                                                
       102 -  streamingEnabled: boolean  (enables v1.1 message_delta incr
           -emental chunks)                                              
       103 -```                                                          
       104 -                                                             
       105 -Request body: `ChatEventFromUser` (see Part B2)              
       106 -                                                             
       107 -Response: Server-Sent Events stream (see Part C)             
       108 -                                                             
       109 -**When to use:** Any user text message or visible user_action
           - (responseRequired: true).                                   
       110 -                                                             
       111 ----                                                          
       112 -                                                             
       113 -### A4. Send Message (Non-Streaming)                         
       114 -                                                             
       115 -```

       329 -                                                             
       330 -## Part C — SSE Protocol                                     
       331 -                                                             
       332 -Every streaming response is a Server-Sent Events stream. Each
           - SSE message has:                                            
       333 -```                                                          
       334 -event: <event_name>\n                                        
       335 -data: <JSON>\n                                               
       336 -\n                                                           
       337 -```                                                          
       338 -                                                             
       339 -### C1. Turn Lifecycle                                       
       340 -                                                             
       341 -**Template intents** (property_search/*, locality_research/tr
           -ending_localities, locality_research/locality_comparison, com
           -parison/compare_localities, portfolio/recommendations, proper
           -ty_detail/similar_properties):                               
       342 -```                                                          
       343 -1. connection_ack                                            
       344 -2. [Phase 1 — Summary, emitted BEFORE fetch]                 
       345 -   message_delta (chunk 0, messageType: "text")   ← summary_n
           -ode streams single chunk                                     
       346 -   chat_event (text, seq 0, sourceMessageState: "IN_PROGRESS"
           -)                                                            
       347 -3. [Phase 2 — Templates, emitted immediately AFTER fetch]    
       348 -   chat_event (template, seq 1, sourceMessageState: "IN_PROGR
           -ESS")                                                        
       349 -   chat_event (template, seq 2, sourceMessageState: "IN_PROGR
           -ESS")   ← if multiple templates                              
       350 -4. [Phase 3 — Followup commentary, LLM-generated]            
       351 -   message_delta ×N                                ← llm_node
           - streams chunks                                              
       352 -   chat_event (text/markdown, seq N, sourceMessageState: "COM
           -PLETED")                                                     
       353 -5. connection_close                                          
       354 -```                                                          
       355 -                                                             
       356 -**Text-only intents** (property_detail/about, price_trends, c
           -ommute_time, FAQ, financial):                                
       357 -```                                                          
       358 -1. connection_ack                                            
       359 -2. [Single phase — LLM is the full response, no summary or te
           -mplates]                                                     
       360 -   message_delta ×N                                ← llm_node
           - streams chunks                                              
       361 -   chat_event (text/markdown, seq 0, sourceMessageState: "COM
           -PLETED")                                                     
       362 -3. connection_close                                          
       363 -```                                                          
       364 -                                                             
       365 -**Short-circuit turns** (Tier 0/1/2, clarification, auth-gate
           -d):                                                          
       366 -```                                                          
       367 -1. connection_ack                                            
       368 -2. chat_event (single event via emit_final_state — sourceMess
           -ageState: "COMPLETED")                                       
       369 -   OR nested_qna / login / share_location template event     
       370 -   (HTTP response closes immediately after — no streaming)   
       371 -3. connection_close                                          
       372 -```                                                          
       373 -                                                             
       374 -**Ordering guarantee:** The graph topology enforces ordering.
           - `summary_node` completes before                             
       375 -`fetch_data_node` starts. `respond_node` (templates) complete
           -s before `llm_node` starts streaming.                        
       376 -The FE receives events in causal order over the same SSE conn
           -ection — no race conditions.                                 
       377 -                                                             
       378 -### C2. connection_ack                                       
       379 -                                                             
       380 -```typescript                                                
       381 -interface ConnectionAck {                                    
       382 -  messageId:    string;  // request_id (UUID4) — identifies t
           -his turn, not a DB message row                               
       383 -  messageState: 'IN_PROGRESS';                               
       384 -}                                                            
       385 -```                                                          
       386 -                                                             
       387 -Emitted immediately when the POST is received. The frontend t
           -reats this as confirmation that                              
       388 -the message was received and shows the user's message in "sen
           -t" state.                                                    
       389 -                                                             
       390 -### C3. chat_event                                           
       391 -                                                             
       392 -A complete `ChatEventToUser` object (see Part B1), serialized
           - as JSON.                                                    
       393 -                                                             
       394 -### C4. message_delta                                        
       395 -                                                             
       396 -A `MessageDeltaEventToUser` object (see Part B3), serialized 
           -as JSON. Only emitted when                                   
       397 -`?streamingEnabled=true` is in the query string.             
       398 -                                                             
       399 -### C5. connection_close                                     
       400 -                                                             
       401 -```json                                                      
       402 -{                                                            
       403 -  "reason": "response_complete" | "inactivity_15s" | "error" 
           -| "cancelled"                                                
       404 -}                                                            
       405 -```                                                          
       406 -                                                             
       407 ----

           -m `property_search/explore_nearby`)

       565 -**Implementation:** `user_location_needed` is a filter key se
           -t by the SLM in `filter_delta`. `derive_node` detects it and 
           -short-circuits: instead of continuing the pipeline, it sets `
           -bot_response` directly with a `share_location` template paylo
           -ad. The runner's `emit_final_state` emits the `chat_event`. N
           -o `get_location` SSE event is emitted.                       
       566 -                                                             
       567 -**Flow:**                                                    
       568 -1. SLM outputs `filter_delta: { user_location_needed: true }`
       569 -2. `derive_node` sees `user_location_needed = true` in filter
           -s

           -peline emits `share_location` template                       
       571 -4. Frontend renders the location permission button

       811 -## Part F — Multi-Event Turn Assembly                        
       812 -                                                             
       813 -A single bot turn produces up to 3 phases of SSE events. All 
           -rows share the same `sourceMessageId`                        
       814 -(= `request_id` for the turn). `sequenceNumber` orders them w
           -ithin the turn. The last event always                        
       815 -has `sourceMessageState: "COMPLETED"` — the FE waits for this
           - before marking the turn done.                               
       816 -                                                             
       817 -### F1. Sequence Model                                       
       818 -                                                             
       819 -**Template intents** (property_search, locality_research, com
           -parison, portfolio, similar_properties):                     
       820 -```                                                          
       821 -sourceMessageId = request_id                                 
       822 -                                                             
       823 -Phase 1 — Summary (summary_node, BEFORE fetch)               
       824 -  message_delta  { messageId: A, sequenceNumber: 0, chunkInde
           -x: 0, content.text: "..." }                                  
       825 -  chat_event     { messageId: A, seq: 0, type: "text",     so
           -urceMessageState: "IN_PROGRESS" }                            
       826 -                                                             
       827 -Phase 2 — Templates (respond_node, AFTER fetch)              
       828 -  chat_event     { messageId: B, seq: 1, type: "template", te
           -mplateId: "property_carousel",                               
       829 -                   sourceMessageState: "IN_PROGRESS" }       
       830 -  chat_event     { messageId: C, seq: 2, type: "template", te
           -mplateId: "locality_carousel",                               
       831 -                   sourceMessageState: "IN_PROGRESS" }   ← IN
           -_PROGRESS even if last template                              
       832 -                                                             
       833 -Phase 3 — Followup (followup_node, AFTER LLM stream)         
       834 -  message_delta ×N  { messageId: D, sequenceNumber: 3, chunkI
           -ndex: 0..N-1, content.text: chunk }                          
       835 -  chat_event     { messageId: D, seq: 3, type: "text",     so
           -urceMessageState: "COMPLETED" }                              
       836 -```                                                          
       837 -                                                             
       838 -**Text-only intents** (property_detail/about, price_trends, c
           -ommute_time, FAQ, financial):                                
       839 -```                                                          
       840 -Phase 1 — skipped (no summary)                               
       841 -Phase 2 — skipped (no templates)                             
       842 -Phase 3 only:                                                
       843 -  message_delta ×N  { messageId: A, sequenceNumber: 0, chunkI
           -ndex: 0..N-1, ... }                                          
       844 -  chat_event     { messageId: A, seq: 0, type: "text/markdown
           -", sourceMessageState: "COMPLETED" }                         
       845 -```                                                          
       846 -

       954 -## Part H — Graph Node Invariant Update                      
       955 -                                                             
       956 -**Current invariant (3-phase model):**                       
       957 -                                                             
       958 -Three graph nodes emit SSE directly: `summary_node`, `respond
           -_node`, and `followup_node`.                                 
       959 -`llm_node` emits `message_delta` chunks. All short-circuit no
           -des only set `bot_response`.                                 
       960 -                                                             
       961 -```                                                          
       962 -connection_ack         ← HTTP handler (before graph)         
       963 -  [summary_node]       ← message_delta + chat_event (text, se
           -q 0)   — BEFORE fetch                                        
       964 -  [respond_node]       ← chat_event × N templates            
           -       — AFTER fetch                                         
       965 -  [llm_node]           ← message_delta × chunks              
           -       — AFTER templates                                     
       966 -  [followup_node]      ← chat_event (text, COMPLETED)        
           -       — AFTER LLM stream                                    
       967 -  OR                                                         
       968 -  [emit_final_state]   ← chat_event (short-circuit paths only
           -)                                                            
       969 -connection_close       ← HTTP handler (after graph)          
       970 -```                                                          
       971 -                                                             
       972 -**Invariant: the FE receives events in strict causal order** 
           -because the graph is a linear chain —                        
       973 -each node runs to completion before the next starts. Summary 
           -always precedes templates; templates                         
       974 -always precede LLM streaming; the COMPLETED marker always arr
           -ives last.                                                   
       975 -                                                             
       976 -**`emit_final_state` fires when:** `bot_response` is set AND 
           -`validated_text is None`.                                    
       977 -`validated_text` is set by `validate_output_node` (which runs
           - after `llm_node`). When it is `None`,                       
       978 -the pipeline short-circuited before reaching the LLM — `follo
           -wup_node` never ran and the short-circuit                    
       979 -node set `bot_response` directly. `emit_final_state` is calle
           -d at the HTTP handler level after graph                      
       980 -exit; it does NOT fire for full-pipeline turns because `valid
           -ated_text` will be non-None on those paths.                  
       981 -                                                             
       982 -**Sequence number assignment:**

⏺ Done. Here's a summary of every decision made and why:

  ---
  Database & schema decisions

  PostgreSQL for conversations + messages (not MongoDB)
  Templates are < 50KB — JSONB handles this cleanly without a second database to
  operate. Monthly partitioning handles the 90-day retention with zero-cost
  DROP TABLE messages_2026_XX (instant, no row locks, ~336GB/month reclaimed).
  MongoDB would add a parallel write path, a second connection pool, and
  operational complexity for no benefit at this payload size.

  Messages partitioned by month, not by conversation_id
  History queries are WHERE conversation_id = X ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 
  20 — the conversation_id + created_at index on each partition covers this
  perfectly. Partition pruning eliminates old months from query planning. If we
  partitioned by conversation_id, we'd need to scan all partitions for any
  query.

  Async write via Kafka — SSE path never touches Postgres
  At 1200 RPS, synchronous Postgres inserts would add 2–5ms to every SSE stream.
  Kafka consumer batches 500 rows and flushes every 100ms — Postgres sees
  ~4,200 rows/second in comfortable batches instead of 1,200 concurrent small
  inserts.

  LLM concurrency gate in Redis (token bucket)
  120 concurrent LLM calls at p50 800ms = 150 completions/second. At 1200 RPS
  chat × 70% LLM rate = 840/second needed — this is a 5.6× overload. The Redis
  atomic EVAL + queue pattern absorbs bursts (up to 300 queued = ~2s of burst),
  sheds gracefully beyond that (503 with Retry-After: 3), and never lets queue
  depth become unbounded.

  Rate limiting at token_id level, not IP
  Housing.com users are mobile-first in India — carrier NAT means many users
  share IPs. Token-level rate limiting is fair and correct.

  Anonymous → logged-in migration is a single UPDATE
  conversation_id never changes. Only user_id is backfilled. Session in Redis is
  patched in-place. No data movement, no new conversation.

  Infrastructure at peak (1200 RPS)
  - 8–12 FastAPI pods (auto-scaled), 4vCPU/8GB each
  - PostgreSQL: r7g.2xlarge primary + r7g.xlarge read replica, 2TB gp3
  - Redis Cluster: 3× r7g.large (13GB each) — 10× headroom intentional
  - Kafka: shared cluster, 12 partitions on chat.messages

  Estimated steady-state storage (90 days)
  ~1TB in PostgreSQL (drops oldest partition monthly), ~1.2GB active data in
  Redis (TTL-bounded), Kafka 24h retention only.

      204  
      205 +### History load query pattern                                
      206 +                                                              
      207 +Loading a conversation page requires two steps:               
      208 +                                                              
      209 +```python                                                     
      210 +# Step 1: Paginated metadata query from PostgreSQL (fast, inde
          +xed)                                                          
      211 +rows = await pg.fetch("""                                     
      212 +    SELECT message_id, message_type, sender_type, message_stat
          +e,                                                            
      213 +           sequence_number, source_message_id, template_id,   
      214 +           content_inline, content_ref, created_at            
      215 +      FROM messages                                           
      216 +     WHERE conversation_id = $1                               
      217 +       AND created_at < $2                                    
      218 +     ORDER BY created_at DESC                                 
      219 +     LIMIT 20                                                 
      220 +""", conversation_id, cursor)                                 
      221 +                                                              
      222 +# Step 2: Bulk fetch template payloads from MongoDB (for rows 
          +with content_ref)                                             
      223 +template_refs = [row['content_ref'] for row in rows if row['co
          +ntent_ref']]                                                  
      224 +if template_refs:                                             
      225 +    template_docs = await mongo.messages_content.find(        
      226 +        {'_id': {'$in': template_refs}},                      
      227 +        projection={'content': 1}                             
      228 +    ).to_list(length=None)                                    
      229 +    content_by_ref = {str(doc['_id']): doc['content'] for doc 
          +in template_docs}                                             
      230 +                                                              
      231 +# Step 3: Merge and return                                    
      232 +result = []                                                   
      233 +for row in rows:                                              
      234 +    if row['content_ref']:                                    
      235 +        payload = content_by_ref.get(str(row['content_ref']), 
          +{})                                                           
      236 +    else:                                                     
      237 +        payload = row['content_inline'] or {}                 
      238 +    result.append({**row, 'content': payload})                
      239 +```                                                           
      240 +                                                              
      241 +The two-step approach adds ~2ms for the MongoDB batch fetch bu
          +t keeps PostgreSQL rows at ~500 bytes vs ~46KB. At 60 history 
          +page loads/second, this is well within latency budget.

      329 +90-day steady state: ~1.5TB compressed (TTL deletes oldest doc

          +mit)

          +load

          +c

          +in-memory

      344 +                                                              
      345 +```python                                                     
      346 +class MongoDbWriter:                                          
      347 +    """Separate Kafka consumer group — only processes template
          + rows."""                                                     
      348 +                                                              
      349 +    async def process_batch(self, records: list[ConsumerRecord
          +]):                                                           
      350 +        template_rows = [r for r in records if r.message_type 
          +== 'template']                                                
      351 +        if not template_rows:                                 
      352 +            return                                            
      353 +                                                              
      354 +        # Dedup                                               
      355 +        unique = [r for r in template_rows                    
      356 +                  if not await redis.exists(f'kafka:mongo:dedu
          +p:{r.content_ref}')]                                          
      357 +                                                              
      358 +        # Bulk insert (ordered=False for parallel insertion)  
      359 +        docs = [{                                             
      360 +            '_id':             r.content_ref,                 
      361 +            'conversation_id': r.conversation_id,             
      362 +            'template_id':     r.template_id,                 
      363 +            'content':         r.content_data,  # the full tem
          +plate payload                                                 
      364 +            'size_bytes':      len(json.dumps(r.content_data))
          +,                                                             
      365 +            'created_at':      r.created_at,                  
      366 +        } for r in unique]                                    
      367 +                                                              
      368 +        if docs:                                              
      369 +            await mongo.messages_content.insert_many(         
      370 +                docs,                                         
      371 +                ordered=False   # continue on duplicate key er
          +rors                                                          
      372 +            )                                                 
      373 +                                                              
      374 +        # Mark dedup (300s window)                            
      375 +        pipe = redis.pipeline()                               
      376 +        for r in unique:                                      
      377 +            pipe.setex(f'kafka:mongo:dedup:{r.content_ref}', 3
          +00, '1')                                                      
      378 +        await pipe.execute()                                  
      379 +```

⏺ Done. Here's a precise summary of what changed and why each decision was made:

  ---
  What changed with the corrected template sizes

  The number that changed everything: Average template payload 40KB (not 3KB as
  assumed before). This shifts daily content writes from 11GB to 35GB — a 3×
  revision.

  Consequence for storage:
  - Postgres-only approach: 35GB/day × 90 days = 3.1TB steady state. Technically
  fine but operationally expensive — large gp3 volumes, slower VACUUM, heavier
  autovacuum, and JSONB parsing overhead on every insert for 750K large
  documents per day.
  - With MongoDB for template payloads only: Postgres drops to 2GB/day (metadata
  + small text rows), MongoDB handles 17GB/day compressed.

  Why MongoDB for templates specifically:
  1. TTL index handles 90-day expiry automatically — MongoDB deletes old
  documents in the background. Postgres needs pg_partman + a partition drop cron
  job.
  2. WiredTiger compression (~2:1 with snappy) cuts 34.5GB/day to ~17GB/day on
  disk.
  3. _id bulk fetches are fast — the only query pattern needed for history loads
  is $in on _id with up to 20 IDs. MongoDB is purpose-built for this.
  4. Already in prod — no new operational surface.

  Schema change: messages table gets content_inline JSONB (for text/user_action
  rows, ~500 bytes) and content_ref UUID (foreign reference to MongoDB, set only
  for template rows). A CHECK constraint ensures exactly one is set per row.
  Kafka has two separate consumer groups — one writes metadata to Postgres, one
  writes payloads to MongoDB.

  Instance sizing revised downward for Postgres, upward for MongoDB:
  - PostgreSQL: was r7g.2xlarge + 2TB → now r7g.xlarge + 500GB (lean metadata
  store)
  - MongoDB: new — r7g.2xlarge + 2TB (handles the bulk of the data)
  - Total storage cost is similar but Postgres is now correctly sized for its
  actual workload

✻ Brewed for 2m 10s

❯ what are we using postres for? not questioning your decision, just want to    
  understand depply, what we'll store and where                                 

⏺ Good question — let me explain the mental model clearly.

  ---
  What PostgreSQL actually stores

  Think of it in two tables.

  conversations — one row per chat session

  This is the history sidebar. When a user opens the app and sees their past
  conversations listed, that comes from this table.

  conversation_id | user_id | status | city    | last_intent    | preview
                    | turn_count | updated_at
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ───────────────────────────────────────
  conv_abc123     | u_4421  | active | Mumbai  | filter_search  | "show me 2bhk
  in powai"         | 12         | 2026-05-29 14:30
  conv_def456     | u_4421  | ended  | Pune    | locality_about | "what's
  Kothrud like?"          | 4          | 2026-05-27 09:15

  Nothing heavy. Just enough to render the sidebar and re-open a conversation.

  ---
  messages — one row per event persisted

  This is every message in every conversation. Two flavours:

  Text rows (user messages, bot text responses, summaries) — content stored
  directly here since it's tiny:

  message_id | conversation_id | type        | sender | content_inline
                            | content_ref
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  msg_001    | conv_abc123     | user_action | user   | {"text": "show me 2bhk
  in powai"}                  | NULL
  msg_002    | conv_abc123     | text        | bot    | {"text": "I see you're
  looking for 2BHK in Powai"} | NULL
  msg_005    | conv_abc123     | text        | bot    | {"text": "47 results —
  good spread from ₹1.2–1.5Cr"}| NULL

  Template rows (property carousel, locality carousel, floor plan) — only a
  pointer here, full payload is in MongoDB:

  message_id | conversation_id | type     | sender | template_id         |
  content_inline | content_ref
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ───────────────────────
  msg_003    | conv_abc123     | template | bot    | property_carousel   | NULL
           | mongo_doc_789
  msg_004    | conv_abc123     | template | bot    | property_carousel   | NULL
           | mongo_doc_790

  content_ref is just a UUID pointer into MongoDB. The actual 40KB property card
  JSON lives there.

  ---
  What queries PostgreSQL serves

  Only two things actually query Postgres at runtime:

  1. History sidebar (user opens the app)
  SELECT conversation_id, preview, city, last_intent, turn_count, updated_at
  FROM conversations
  WHERE user_id = 'u_4421'
  ORDER BY updated_at DESC
  LIMIT 20;

  2. Paginated message load (user opens a past conversation)
  SELECT message_id, message_type, sender_type, template_id,
         content_inline, content_ref, created_at
  FROM messages
  WHERE conversation_id = 'conv_abc123'
    AND created_at < '2026-05-29 14:30:00'   -- cursor
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 20;

  For text rows — content is right there, done. For template rows — app sees
  content_ref, does a batch MongoDB lookup for those UUIDs, stitches the
  payloads in, and returns the full page to the frontend.

  ---
  Why Postgres and not MongoDB for this?

  MongoDB could technically do this, but these two queries are why Postgres wins
  here:

  The history sidebar needs WHERE user_id = X ORDER BY updated_at DESC. That's a
  B-tree index scan — Postgres is purpose-built for this and does it in
  microseconds. MongoDB can also index this but with higher overhead for the
  write path and no native partitioned-table semantics.

  Pagination needs WHERE conversation_id = X AND created_at < cursor. Again a
  compound B-tree index, one I/O per page. This is the canonical relational
  access pattern.

  Monthly partitions let us drop old data instantly — DROP TABLE 
  messages_2026_02 takes milliseconds regardless of how many millions of rows
  are in it. Row-by-row deletes at 3.5M rows/day would be a constant VACUUM
  nightmare.

  Counters and updates — UPDATE conversations SET turn_count = turn_count + 1 is
  a simple atomic operation in Postgres. In MongoDB you'd use $inc which works
  but adds coordination complexity.

  ---
  The full picture of what lives where

  ┌────────────┬────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
  │   Store    │              What              │         Why here          │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │            │                                │ Relational queries (list  │
  │ PostgreSQL │ Conversation list + message    │ by user, paginate by      │
  │            │ metadata + text content        │ date), tiny rows, ACID,   │
  │            │                                │ fast partition drops      │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │            │ Template payloads              │ Large documents, _id bulk │
  │ MongoDB    │ (property/locality/floor plan  │  lookup, built-in TTL for │
  │            │ cards)                         │  90-day expiry,           │
  │            │                                │ WiredTiger compression    │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │            │ Live session state (filters,   │ Sub-ms reads, TTL-native, │
  │ Redis      │ entities, turn history, LLM    │  atomic counters, pub/sub │
  │            │ queue)                         │  for LLM queue signalling │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │            │ In-flight messages before DB   │ Decouples SSE response    │
  │ Kafka      │ write                          │ from DB latency; async,   │
  │            │                                │ ordered, replayable       │
  └────────────┴────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

  Everything the user sees (history list, conversation messages) comes from
  Postgres + MongoDB. Everything the bot needs to process the next message comes
  from Redis. Postgres never touches the hot path — it only answers when a user
  browses history.

✻ Worked for 47s

❯ let say page loads and user history is loaded. that means two calls first to  
  postgres to get the message, then to mongo to get the detailed templated      
  responses. this happens sequentially. then stiching the responses together    
  and sending them. is it not too much?                                         

⏺ You're right to question it. Let me think through this honestly.

  The two-step approach adds:
  - ~3–5ms MongoDB round-trip (fast since it's cached)
  - Code complexity — two queries, stitching logic
  - Two failure points — if MongoDB is down, history breaks entirely
  - Two connection pools in every app pod

  The reason I introduced the split was when I thought templates were 35GB/day →
  3TB+ in Postgres — at that scale the split made operational sense. But at the
  corrected 15GB/day → ~1.1TB over 90 days, Postgres handles it cleanly without
  needing MongoDB at all.

  And there's no VACUUM concern either — messages are append-only. VACUUM only
  touches rows that were UPDATEd or DELETEd. We never update message content,
  and we drop entire monthly partitions instead of deleting rows. Postgres has
  no bloat problem here.

  The correct answer: drop MongoDB from this service. One database, one query.

         +pools, and stitching code. If MongoDB is down, history breaks e
         +ntirely.                                                       
       9  
      13 -If Housing.com's MongoDB cluster has spare capacity (likely, si
         -nce it's shared infra), the split costs nothing operationally. 
         -If simplicity is the priority, a Postgres-only approach with mo
         -nthly partitions and 1TB gp3 SSD is also viable. **This documen
         -t specifies the hybrid approach as the production recommendatio
         -n.**                                                           
      10 +**Messages are append-only** — no UPDATEs on content, no DELETE
         + storms. Postgres VACUUM only touches updated or deleted rows. 
         +Monthly partition drops handle retention as `DROP TABLE message
         +s_2026_02` (instant, no vacuum, no bloat). The theoretical VACU
         +UM concern doesn't apply here.

⏺ Clean. 583 lines, single database, no stitching. Here's the plain summary of
  what changed and why:

  ---
  What changed (and the honest reasoning)

  MongoDB dropped entirely from this service.

  The two-step load you identified — Postgres → MongoDB → stitch → return —
  would have been:
  - ~5ms extra per history page (MongoDB batch lookup, even cached)
  - Code that stitches two query results together
  - Two failure points: if MongoDB goes down, every history page breaks
  - Two connection pools in every pod
  - Two consumer groups in Kafka with different processing logic

  None of that overhead is justified. At 15GB/day of template content (corrected
  from 35GB), PostgreSQL with a 2.5TB gp3 SSD and monthly partition drops
  handles it cleanly.

  The key insight about VACUUM that makes this safe: messages are append-only.
  PostgreSQL's VACUUM only works on rows that have been UPDATEd or DELETEd — it
  has nothing to do on this table. The large JSONB content column never causes
  bloat because it's never modified after insert. Monthly DROP TABLE 
  messages_2026_XX instantly reclaims ~500GB without touching any live data.

  Final architecture for history load:
  SELECT message_id, message_type, content, ...
  FROM messages
  WHERE conversation_id = $1 AND created_at < $2
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

  One query. Full content including 40KB template cards inline. Done.

      584 +                                                              
      585 +---                                                           
      586 +                                                              
      587 +## 12. Mental Model — Why This Architecture and How to Think A
          +bout It                                                       
      588 +                                                              
      589 +### The two questions that drive every storage decision       
      590 +                                                              
      591 +Every storage decision in this system traces back to two quest
          +ions:                                                         
      592 +                                                              
      593 +**1. Who reads this data, how often, and in what shape?**     
      594 +**2. How painful is it to change the write path vs the read pa
          +th?**                                                         
      595 +                                                              
      596 +For chat history: users browse their own history occasionally 
          +(not every session), the access pattern is always `conversatio
          +n_id + time cursor → page of messages`, and the read needs to 
          +return complete renderable data in one shot (no FE-side assemb
          +ly). That's a textbook relational pagination query. PostgreSQL
          + is the right answer.                                         
      597 +                                                              
      598 +For session state: the bot reads and updates it on *every sing
          +le turn*, needs sub-millisecond access, and the data is inhere
          +ntly ephemeral (if Redis goes down, the user just starts a new
          + session — no data loss that matters). That's Redis.          
      599 +                                                              
      600 +For write throughput isolation: you don't want a slow Postgres
          + insert to make the user wait 50ms more for an SSE event. That
          +'s Kafka.                                                     
      601 +                                                              
      602 +---                                                           
      603 +                                                              
      604 +### Why PostgreSQL for large JSONB isn't the scary thing it so
          +unds like                                                     
      605 +                                                              
      606 +The concern with storing 40–100KB JSONB in PostgreSQL usually 
          +comes from one of three places:                               
      607 +                                                              
      608 +**Fear 1: "JSONB is slow to write."**                         
      609 +JSONB parsing cost at insert is ~microseconds for a 100KB docu
          +ment. At our write throughput (Kafka consumer, batched), this 
          +is invisible. The bottleneck is disk I/O and network, not JSON
          + parsing.                                                     
      610 +                                                              
      611 +**Fear 2: "Bloat — JSONB updates cause table bloat, need frequ
          +ent VACUUM."**                                                
      612 +This is true for tables with frequent UPDATEs. Our messages ta
          +ble is **append-only** — content is written once and never tou
          +ched again. VACUUM has nothing to do. There is no dead tuple a
          +ccumulation, no bloat, no autovacuum thrash. This is the singl
          +e most important property of our schema.                      
      613 +                                                              
      614 +**Fear 3: "Storing 100KB per row will make queries slow."**   
      615 +A history page load fetches 20 rows. Even if all 20 are 100KB 
          +templates, that's 2MB of data. PostgreSQL returns this from a 
          +single sequential scan of 20 rows within one partition. It's f
          +ast because the query is index-scan → sequential fetch within 
          +an index-range, not a full table scan. The `(conversation_id, 
          +created_at DESC)` index makes this O(log N + 20) regardless of
          + how many rows exist.                                         
      616 +                                                              
      617 +---                                                           
      618 +                                                              
      619 +### The partition drop is the key operational insight         
      620 +                                                              
      621 +Traditional retention logic: run a DELETE every night, deal wi
          +th bloat, deal with VACUUM, deal with replication lag.        
      622 +                                                              
      623 +Partition drop logic: `DROP TABLE messages_2026_01`. This is a
          + metadata operation. It takes milliseconds. It doesn't lock th
          +e parent table (no impact on live queries). It doesn't generat
          +e WAL proportional to the data size. It reclaims ~500GB of dis
          +k instantly. PostgreSQL forgets the partition exists.         
      624 +                                                              
      625 +This changes the calculus significantly. You can store more in
          + Postgres than feels instinctively safe because you know the c
          +leanup is free.                                               
      626 +                                                              
      627 +---                                                           
      628 +                                                              
      629 +### The two-database pattern: when it helps, when it hurts    
      630 +                                                              
      631 +The intuition behind a Postgres + MongoDB split is: keep Postg
          +res lean (fast queries, small rows, fits in shared_buffers) an
          +d let MongoDB absorb large documents.                         
      632 +                                                              
      633 +This is correct at certain scales. It starts hurting when:    
      634 +- **Every read requires both databases.** There's no read path
          + that needs only the MongoDB data — you always need the Postgr
          +es metadata first. So every history page load becomes: Postgre
          +s query → extract refs → MongoDB batch fetch → stitch. Sequent
          +ial, two failure modes, stitching code.                       
      635 +- **The data volume doesn't justify it.** At 15GB/day, Postgre
          +s steady state is ~2.2TB over 90 days. A single r7g.2xlarge wi
          +th a 2.5TB gp3 SSD handles this. The MongoDB cluster you'd spi
          +n up to "save" Postgres would be a larger instance than the Po
          +stgres upgrade you avoided.                                   
      636 +- **You already have partitioning.** The main scaling lever fo
          +r Postgres is partition management. With monthly partitions yo
          +u're dropping 500GB per month with zero operational cost. Mong
          +oDB's TTL index is elegant, but it's solving the same problem 
          +Postgres partitioning already solves.                         
      637 +                                                              
      638 +The split becomes worthwhile when: content/day > ~30GB (templa
          +te frequency increases or sizes grow), OR when steady-state st
          +orage exceeds ~3TB and gp3 SSD costs become significant, OR wh
          +en you need cross-collection queries that MongoDB handles bett
          +er.                                                           
      639 +                                                              
      640 +---                                                           
      641 +                                                              
      642 +### How to think about each store's "job"                     
      643 +                                                              
      644 +```                                                           
      645 +PostgreSQL  =  The ledger                                     
      646 +               Durable, ordered, queryable. Answers "what happ
          +ened in this conversation?"                                   
      647 +               Optimised for: paginated access by conversation
          + + time.                                                      
      648 +                                                              
      649 +Redis       =  Working memory                                 
      650 +               Fast, ephemeral, shared. Answers "what does the
          + bot need right now?"                                         
      651 +               Optimised for: sub-ms reads, TTL expiry, atomic
          + operations.                                                  
      652 +               Not a backup for anything — data loss is surviv
          +able.                                                         
      653 +                                                              
      654 +Kafka       =  The delivery truck                             
      655 +               Ordered, durable in-transit. Bridges the SSE pa
          +th to the DB write path.                                      
      656 +               Optimised for: decoupling latency, absorbing wr
          +ite bursts, replay.                                           
      657 +                                                              
      658 +MongoDB     =  The document warehouse (not used yet)          
      659 +               Horizontal scale for large documents. Shines wh
          +en you need to store                                          
      660 +               millions of large, heterogeneous documents and 
          +access them by _id.                                           
      661 +               The right choice when Postgres JSONB storage > 
          +~3TB steady state.

          +Split
