          +hange)                                                        
      772 +

      774 +- Reads from `chat.messages` topic (same as existing group)   
      775 +- Filters for `message_type = 'template'` rows only           
      776 +- Inserts template payloads into MongoDB `messages_content` co

      777 +

      779 +                                                              
      780 +```                                                           
      781 +Status after Phase 1:                                         
      782 +  Postgres:  all rows (text + templates in content JSONB)

          + date                                                         
      784 +  Read path: unchanged (still Postgres-only)

      788 +

      790 +

          +ng)                                                           
      792 +

      794 +ALTER TABLE messages ADD COLUMN content_ref UUID;             
      795 +-- NULL for all existing rows. No data migration yet.         
      796 +-- No index yet — only add when reads switch over.            
      797 +```                                                           
      798 +                                                              
      799 +Update the Kafka Postgres consumer to also populate `content_r
          +ef` for new template rows (same UUID as the MongoDB `_id`):   
      800 +```python                                                     
      801 +if row.message_type == 'template':                            
      802 +    row.content_ref = row.content_data['_id']   # same UUID wr
          +itten to both stores                                          
      803 +```                                                           
      804 +                                                              
      805 +```

          +nt (both set)                                                 
      808 +  MongoDB:  template rows from Phase 1 onwards                
      809 +  Read path: unchanged                                        
      810 +```

      812 +---                                                           
      813 +                                                              
      814 +### Phase 3 — Backfill historical MongoDB documents           
      815 +                                                              
      816 +For template rows older than Phase 1 deployment, backfill Mong
          +oDB from Postgres:                                            
      817 +                                                              
      818 +```python                                                     
      819 +# Run as a background job, off-peak hours                     
      820 +# Process in batches of 1,000 rows per partition              
      821 +                                                              
      822 +for partition in monthly_partitions_after_cutoff:             
      823 +    for batch in pg.stream("""                                
      824 +        SELECT message_id, conversation_id, template_id, conte
          +nt, created_at                                                
      825 +          FROM {partition}                                    
      826 +         WHERE message_type = 'template'                      
      827 +           AND content_ref IS NULL                            
      828 +    """):                                                     
      829 +        docs = [{'_id': row.message_id, 'conversation_id': row
          +.conversation_id,                                             
      830 +                 'template_id': row.template_id, 'content': ro
          +w.content['data'],                                            
      831 +                 'created_at': row.created_at}                
      832 +                for row in batch]                             
      833 +        mongo.messages_content.insert_many(docs, ordered=False
          +)                                                             
      834 +                                                              
      835 +        pg.execute("""                                        
      836 +            UPDATE {partition}                                
      837 +               SET content_ref = message_id                   
      838 +             WHERE message_id = ANY($1)                       
      839 +               AND message_type = 'template'                  
      840 +        """, [row.message_id for row in batch])               
      841 +```                                                           
      842 +                                                              
      843 +**Important:** The UPDATE on historical partitions WILL genera
          +te VACUUM work. Run this during low-traffic periods. Monitor a
          +utovacuum.                                                    
      844 +                                                              
      845 +**Validation gate:** `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM messages WHERE mess
          +age_type = 'template' AND content_ref IS NULL` returns 0 befor
          +e proceeding.                                                 
      846 +

      848 +                                                              
      849 +### Phase 4 — Switch reads to use MongoDB for template rows   
      850 +                                                              
      851 +Update the history load query handler:                        
      852 +                                                              
      853 +```python                                                     
      854 +# Before (Postgres-only)                                      
      855 +rows = await pg.fetch("SELECT ... content ... FROM messages WH
          +ERE ...")                                                     
      856 +return rows                                                   
      857 +                                                              
      858 +# After (hybrid read)                                         
      859 +rows = await pg.fetch("SELECT ... content_ref, content ... FRO
          +M messages WHERE ...")                                        
      860 +                                                              
      861 +template_refs = [row['content_ref'] for row in rows if row['co
          +ntent_ref']]                                                  
      862 +if template_refs:                                             
      863 +    docs = await mongo.messages_content.find(                 
      864 +        {'_id': {'$in': template_refs}}, {'content': 1}       
      865 +    ).to_list()                                               
      866 +    content_map = {str(d['_id']): d['content'] for d in docs} 
      867 +                                                              
      868 +for row in rows:                                              
      869 +    if row['content_ref']:                                    
      870 +        row['content'] = {'templateId': row['template_id'],   
      871 +                          'data': content_map.get(str(row['con
          +tent_ref']), {})}                                             
      872 +```                                                           
      873 +                                                              
      874 +Deploy behind a feature flag. A/B test: compare history load l
          +atency Postgres-only vs hybrid. If latency is acceptable, roll
          + out to 100%.                                                 
      875 +                                                              
      876 +**Rollback:** Disable feature flag. Reads fall back to Postgre
          +s-only. Postgres still has `content` intact.                  
      877 +                                                              
      878 +---                                                           
      879 +                                                              
      880 +### Phase 5 — Null out Postgres content for template rows (sto
          +rage reclaim)                                                 
      881 +                                                              
      882 +Only do this after Phase 4 is fully stable and rolled out. **T
          +his step is destructive.**                                    
      883 +                                                              
      884 +```sql                                                        
      885 +-- Null out content for template rows, partition by partition 
      886 +-- Run during maintenance window; generates VACUUM work       
      887 +UPDATE messages_2026_01                                       
      888 +   SET content = '{}'::jsonb    -- or NULL if column allows   
      889 + WHERE message_type = 'template'                              
      890 +   AND content_ref IS NOT NULL;                               
      891 +                                                              
      892 +-- Re-run pg_partman maintenance to trigger VACUUM on modified
          + partition                                                    
      893 +SELECT partman.run_maintenance('public.messages');            
      894 +```                                                           
      895 +                                                              
      896 +**After Phase 5:** Storage reclaim begins. Each partition drop
          +s from ~516GB to ~50GB as template JSONB is cleared. Autovacuu
          +m reclaims the freed space.                                   
      897 +                                                              
      898 +---                                                           
      899 +                                                              
      900 +### Phase 6 — Cleanup (optional, do after 30 days stable)     
      901 +                                                              
      902 +- Remove Postgres consumer's template content write (no longer
          + write `content` for template rows)                           
      903 +- Keep `content_ref` column and index as the permanent pattern
      904 +- Update `CONSTRAINT chk_content_xor` to enforce the split at 
          +DB level                                                      
      905 +                                                              
      906 +---                                                           
      907 +                                                              
      908 +### Rollback at each phase                                    
      909 +                                                              
      910 +| Phase | Rollback |                                          
      911 +|---|---|                                                     
      912 +| Phase 1 | Stop `chat-mongo-writer` consumer group. No Postgr
          +es change. |                                                  
      913 +| Phase 2 | `ALTER TABLE messages DROP COLUMN content_ref;`. N
          +o data loss. |                                                
      914 +| Phase 3 | No rollback needed — backfill is additive only. | 
      915 +| Phase 4 | Disable feature flag. Reads use Postgres. |       
      916 +| Phase 5 | **Cannot rollback** — Postgres content has been cl
          +eared. Only roll to Phase 5 when MongoDB is proven stable for 
          +30+ days. |                                                   
      917 +                                                              
      918 +---                                                           
      919 +                                                              
      920 +### Reverse migration — MongoDB → Postgres-only (if numbers dr
          +op)                                                           
      921 +                                                              
      922 +If template frequency drops significantly (e.g. templates move
          + out of scope, or product changes):                           
      923 +                                                              
      924 +1. Re-populate `content` from MongoDB for all rows with `conte

      926 +3. Switch reads back to Postgres-only (reverse Phase 4)

      930 +This is simpler than the forward migration because you're goin

⏺ 930 lines, clean structure. Here's what was added and what each section does:

  ---
  What was added

  Section 12 — Mental Model

  Explains the reasoning layer behind the architecture, not just the decisions.
  Three specific fears developers commonly have about Postgres + JSONB are
  addressed head-on:

  - "JSONB is slow to write" — microseconds of parsing cost, invisible at batch
  insert scale
  - "Bloat and VACUUM problems" — only applies to tables with UPDATEs. Messages
  are append-only. VACUUM has nothing to do here.
  - "Large rows make queries slow" — history load is a 20-row index scan, not a
  table scan. It's fast regardless of row size.

  The partition drop insight is called out explicitly because it's the single
  most important property of the schema — dropping a monthly partition is a
  metadata operation that takes milliseconds, reclaims 500GB, touches nothing
  live.

  The two-database pattern's failure mode is also documented — when it hurts
  (sequential read dependency, every read needs both stores) so devs understand
  it's not categorically bad, just wrong at this scale.

  ---
  Section 13 — Decision Framework (Q&A)

  Six concrete questions, each with thresholds derived from the capacity math:

  ┌─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        Question         │               Trigger threshold               │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Monthly content         │ > 1TB/month → MongoDB split                   │
  │ growing?                │                                               │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Template payload sizes? │ p95 > 200KB → MongoDB split (TOAST off-page   │
  │                         │ reads degrade)                                │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ History load latency?   │ p95 > 150ms after caching → MongoDB split     │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Storage cost?           │ > $320/month → evaluate split                 │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Template frequency much │ < 10% → quarterly partitions, simpler         │
  │  lower?                 │ maintenance                                   │
  ├─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Write throughput?       │ Kafka lag > 10K sustained → scale consumers   │
  │                         │ or profile INSERTs                            │
  └─────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  The compact decision tree at the end is the one thing a dev should look at
  first — three yes/no questions, action is unambiguous.

  ---
  Section 14 — Migration Playbook

  Six-phase live migration with zero downtime:

  1. Deploy MongoDB writer (parallel write, Postgres unchanged) — fully 
  reversible
  2. Add content_ref column to Postgres — fully reversible
  3. Backfill historical rows into MongoDB — additive, no risk
  4. Switch reads to hybrid (feature-flagged) — fully reversible
  5. Null out Postgres content for templates — destructive, only after 30 days 
  stable
  6. Cleanup

  The rollback column at each phase is the important part — a dev can see
  exactly what "undo" means at any point before committing. Phase 5 is
  explicitly marked as the point of no return.

  The reverse migration (MongoDB → Postgres-only) is also documented because if
  template frequency drops — say templates get moved to a CDN or product removes
  them — the split becomes unnecessary complexity and you'd want to consolidate
  back.

          -uches the SSE hot path.

      302 -## 4. Kafka Topics                                            
      303 -                                                              
      304 -Kafka decouples the SSE response path from database writes. Ap
          -plication writes to Kafka and the SSE stream continues — Postg
          -reSQL writes happen asynchronously.                           
      305 -                                                              
      306 -```                                                           
      307 -Topic: chat.messages                                          
      308 -  Partitions: 12 (keyed by conversation_id — order preserved p
          -er conversation)                                              
      309 -  Replication factor: 3                                       
      310 -  Retention: 24h                                              
      311 -  Payload (text rows):     { message_id, conversation_id, mess
          -age_type, sender_type,                                        
      312 -                             message_state, sequence_number, s
          -ource_message_id,                                             
      313 -                             template_id, content, request_id,
          - created_at }                                                 
      314 -                             avg ~2KB per message             
      315 -                                                              
      316 -  Payload (template rows): same shape — content field contains
          - the full 40–100KB                                            
      317 -                           template payload                   
      318 -                                                              
      319 -  Peak throughput:                                            
      320 -    Text rows:     ~3,800/sec × ~2KB     = ~7.6MB/sec         
      321 -    Template rows: ~400/sec  × ~46KB     = ~18.4MB/sec        
      322 -    Total:                               = ~26MB/sec          
      323 -                                                              
      324 -  Note: Kafka handles 100MB/sec+ per broker. Well within share
          -d cluster capacity.                                           
      325 -                                                              
      326 -Topic: chat.session_events                                    
      327 -  Partitions: 6, Replication: 3, Retention: 24h

          -nt,

          -}                                                             
      330 -  Peak: ~1,200 events/sec

      332 -Topic: chat.metrics

      429 -## 6. Capacity Planning                                       
      430 -                                                              
      431 -### Application servers (FastAPI + LangGraph)                 
      432 -                                                              
      433 -```                                                           
      434 -Per pod: 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM → handles ~175 RPS (async, I/O bound)
      435 -At 1200 RPS: 1200 / 175 = ~7 pods needed                      
      436 -Recommendation: min=3, max=12 (HPA on CPU + request latency)  
      437 -Instance: c7g.xlarge (4 vCPU, 8GB) — headroom for GC, startup,
          - connection pools                                             
      438 -```                                                           
      439 -                                                              
      440 -### PostgreSQL                                                
      441 -                                                              
      442 -```                                                           
      443 -Writes: ~4,200 rows/sec peak via Kafka batches of 500         
      444 -Reads:  ~60 history page loads/sec (never on the LLM hot path)
      445 -                                                              
      446 -Storage growth:                                               
      447 -  ~17GB/day raw content + ~0.2GB/day metadata = ~17.2GB/day   
      448 -  90-day raw: ~1.55TB                                         
      449 -  With WAL, indexes, bloat (+40%): ~2.2TB steady state        
      450 -                                                              
      451 -Partition drops free ~17.2GB × 30 = ~516GB per monthly partiti
          -on dropped.                                                   
      452 -                                                              
      453 -Primary:      r7g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64GB RAM) + 2.5TB gp3 SSD  
      454 -Read replica: r7g.xlarge  (4 vCPU, 32GB RAM) + 2.5TB gp3 SSD  
      455 -                                                              
      456 -64GB RAM: shared_buffers = 16GB (covers active partition hot r
          -ows)                                                          
      457 -          effective_cache_size = 48GB                         
      458 -PgBouncer: transaction mode, 100 server connections (primary) 
          -+ 50 (replica)                                                
      459 -```                                                           
      460 -                                                              
      461 -### Redis                                                     
      462 -                                                              
      463 -```                                                           
      464 -Active data: ~1.2GB (see Section 3)                           
      465 -Peak ops/sec: ~7,300 (session R/W + tool cache + LLM gate + ra
          -te limiting)                                                  
      466 -Redis handles 100K+ ops/sec — not the bottleneck.             
      467 -                                                              
      468 -Cluster: 3 primary + 3 replica × r7g.large (13GB each) = ~78GB
          - total                                                        
      469 -```                                                           
      470 -                                                              
      471 -### Kafka                                                     
      472 -                                                              
      473 -```                                                           
      474 -Peak throughput: ~26MB/sec on chat.messages                   
      475 -Partition count: 12 — 12 parallel consumer instances          
      476 -Consumer replicas: 3 (chat-db-writer group)                   
      477 -Lag alert: > 10,000 messages → page on-call                   
      478 -```                                                           
      479 -

      481 -

          -|                                                             
      485 -| Redis | ~1.2GB active | ~1.2GB TTL-bounded | 3× r7g.large cl
          -uster |

      490 -## 7. Write Path (Async via Kafka)                            
      491 -                                                              
      492 -```                                                           
      493 -User message arrives (POST /chat/send-message)                
      494 -        │                                                     
      495 -        ▼                                                     
      496 -FastAPI handler                                               
      497 -  1. Load session from Redis (~1ms)                      ← blo
          -cking: pipeline needs context                                 
      498 -  2. Publish user message → Kafka (chat.messages)        ← fir
          -e-and-forget                                                  
      499 -  3. Run LangGraph pipeline → SSE stream to FE           ← ~80
          -0ms–4s                                                        
      500 -  4. Publish bot messages → Kafka (chat.messages)        ← fir
          -e-and-forget                                                  
      501 -     (includes template payloads up to 100KB in content field)
      502 -  5. HTTP response stream closes                              
      503 -                                                              
      504 -Kafka consumer (chat-db-writer, 3 replicas):                  
      505 -  1. Accumulate 500 messages or 100ms                         
      506 -  2. Dedup check (Redis)                                      
      507 -  3. Bulk INSERT to PostgreSQL messages                       
      508 -  4. Mark dedup keys in Redis                                 
      509 -  5. Commit offset                                            
      510 -                                                              
      511 -Kafka consumer (chat-session-events):                         
      512 -  1. session_start  → INSERT into conversations               
      513 -  2. turn_complete  → UPDATE conversations (turn_count, update
          -d_at, last_intent)                                            
      514 -  3. session_end    → UPDATE conversations SET status = 'ended
          -'                                                             
      515 -```                                                           
      516 -                                                              
      517 -**Why not write synchronously?**                              
      518 -At 1200 RPS: 4,200 INSERT ops/second on the critical path. Eac
          -h INSERT ~2–5ms. Under load, Postgres write latency spikes to 
          -20–50ms → SSE stream latency spike → user perceives lag. Kafka
          - consumer batches to ~500 rows per INSERT cycle, runs asynchro
          -nously, and completely decouples user-facing latency from writ
          -e throughput.                                                 
      519 -                                                              
      520 -**Durability tradeoff:** Kafka `acks=all` — message is durable
          - in Kafka before the handler gets an ack. If a pod dies after 
          -Kafka ack but before SSE delivery: Kafka consumer writes to Po
          -stgres anyway. If pod dies after SSE but before Kafka ack: mes
          -sage lost (< 1s window). Acceptable for chat history.         
      521 -                                                              
      522 ----                                                           
      523 -                                                              
      524 -## 8. Partition Maintenance                                   
      525 -                                                              
      526 -```sql                                                        
      527 --- Nightly via pg_cron:                                       
      528 -SELECT cron.schedule('0 3 * * *', $$SELECT partman.run_mainten
          -ance('public.messages')$$);                                   
      529 --- Creates next 3 months of partitions, drops partitions older
          - than 90 days.                                                
      530 --- DROP TABLE messages_2026_01 is instant — no row scans, no V
          -ACUUM, no locks on active data.                               
      531 -```                                                           
      532 -                                                              
      533 -Partition naming: `messages_YYYY_MM` (e.g. `messages_2026_05`)
          -.                                                             
      534 -Storage reclaimed per drop: ~17.2GB × 30 = ~516GB per monthly 
          -partition.                                                    
      535 -                                                              
      536 ----                                                           
      537 -                                                              
      538 -## 9. Anonymous → Logged-in Migration                         
      539 -                                                              
      540 -`conversation_id` is never replaced. Only `user_id` is backfil
          -led when the user logs in.                                    
      541 -                                                              
      542 -```sql                                                        
      543 -UPDATE conversations                                          
      544 -   SET user_id    = $1,      -- logged-in user_id             
      545 -       updated_at = NOW()                                     
      546 - WHERE token_id = $2                                          
      547 -   AND user_id IS NULL;                                       
      548 -```                                                           
      549 -                                                              
      550 -```python                                                     
      551 -# Redis session patch (in-place — no new session)             
      552 -session = json.loads(await redis.get(f'session:{session_id}'))
      553 -session['user_id']    = new_user_id                           
      554 -session['auth_token'] = new_auth_token                        
      555 -await redis.setex(f'session:{session_id}', 86400, json.dumps(s
          -ession))                                                      
      556 -```

      560 -## 10. Connection Pool Sizing                                 
      561 -                                                              
      562 -```python                                                     
      563 -# PostgreSQL via PgBouncer (transaction mode)                 
      564 -PG_POOL_SIZE    = 10   # per app pod; 10 × 12 pods = 120 → PgB
          -ouncer queues the rest                                        
      565 -PG_MAX_OVERFLOW = 5                                           
      566 -PG_TIMEOUT_S    = 5    # give up after 5s (should never hit un
          -der normal load)                                              
      567 -                                                              
      568 -# Redis Cluster (async client, one pool per shard)            
      569 -REDIS_POOL_SIZE = 20   # per pod                              
      570 -```                                                           
      571 -                                                              
      572 -Kafka consumer (chat-db-writer) is a separate deployment — 3 r
          -eplicas, each with 1 PgBouncer connection for bulk batch inser
          -ts.

      575 -                                                              
      576 -## 11. Database Selection Rationale                           
      577 -                                                              
      578 -| Store | Used for | Key reason |                             
      579 -|---|---|---|                                                 
      580 -| **PostgreSQL** | All persistent chat data — conversations, m
          -essages (text + template content) | Single query for history l
          -oad. Relational pagination. Monthly partition drops for retent
          -ion. Append-only messages = zero VACUUM overhead on content co
          -lumn. |                                                       
      581 -| **Redis** | Session state, LLM concurrency gate, tool cache,
          - rate limiting | Sub-ms reads, atomic counters (INCR/DECR), TT
          -L-native, pub/sub for LLM queue. Not durable — Redis loss only
          - affects in-flight sessions, not history. |                   
      582 -| **Kafka** | Async write pipeline | Decouples SSE latency fro
          -m DB write latency. Ordered delivery per conversation. Replaya
          -ble if consumer crashes. Already in prod. |                   
      583 -| **MongoDB** | Not used | The two-step history load (Postgres
          - → MongoDB → stitch) adds latency, complexity, and two failure
          - points. At 15GB/day template content and 90-day retention, Po
          -stgreSQL handles it comfortably with partitioning. |          
      584 -                                                              
      585 ----                                                           
      586 -                                                              
      587 -## 12. Mental Model — Why This Architecture and How to Think A
          -bout It                                                       
      588 -                                                              
      589 -### The two questions that drive every storage decision       
      590 -                                                              
      591 -Every storage decision in this system traces back to two quest
          -ions:                                                         
      592 -                                                              
      593 -**1. Who reads this data, how often, and in what shape?**     
      594 -**2. How painful is it to change the write path vs the read pa
          -th?**                                                         
      595 -                                                              
      596 -For chat history: users browse their own history occasionally 
          -(not every session), the access pattern is always `conversatio
          -n_id + time cursor → page of messages`, and the read needs to 
          -return complete renderable data in one shot (no FE-side assemb
          -ly). That's a textbook relational pagination query. PostgreSQL
          - is the right answer.                                         
      597 -                                                              
      598 -For session state: the bot reads and updates it on *every sing
          -le turn*, needs sub-millisecond access, and the data is inhere
          -ntly ephemeral (if Redis goes down, the user just starts a new
          - session — no data loss that matters). That's Redis.          
      599 -                                                              
      600 -For write throughput isolation: you don't want a slow Postgres
          - insert to make the user wait 50ms more for an SSE event. That
          -'s Kafka.                                                     
      601 -                                                              
      602 ----                                                           
      603 -                                                              
      604 -### Why PostgreSQL for large JSONB isn't the scary thing it so
          -unds like                                                     
      605 -                                                              
      606 -The concern with storing 40–100KB JSONB in PostgreSQL usually 
          -comes from one of three places:                               
      607 -                                                              
      608 -**Fear 1: "JSONB is slow to write."**                         
      609 -JSONB parsing cost at insert is ~microseconds for a 100KB docu
          -ment. At our write throughput (Kafka consumer, batched), this 
          -is invisible. The bottleneck is disk I/O and network, not JSON
          - parsing.                                                     
      610 -                                                              
      611 -**Fear 2: "Bloat — JSONB updates cause table bloat, need frequ
          -ent VACUUM."**                                                
      612 -This is true for tables with frequent UPDATEs. Our messages ta
          -ble is **append-only** — content is written once and never tou
          -ched again. VACUUM has nothing to do. There is no dead tuple a
          -ccumulation, no bloat, no autovacuum thrash. This is the singl
          -e most important property of our schema.                      
      613 -                                                              
      614 -**Fear 3: "Storing 100KB per row will make queries slow."**   
      615 -A history page load fetches 20 rows. Even if all 20 are 100KB 
          -templates, that's 2MB of data. PostgreSQL returns this from a 
          -single sequential scan of 20 rows within one partition. It's f
          -ast because the query is index-scan → sequential fetch within 
          -an index-range, not a full table scan. The `(conversation_id, 
          -created_at DESC)` index makes this O(log N + 20) regardless of
          - how many rows exist.                                         
      616 -                                                              
      617 ----                                                           
      618 -                                                              
      619 -### The partition drop is the key operational insight         
      620 -                                                              
      621 -Traditional retention logic: run a DELETE every night, deal wi
          -th bloat, deal with VACUUM, deal with replication lag.        
      622 -                                                              
      623 -Partition drop logic: `DROP TABLE messages_2026_01`. This is a
          - metadata operation. It takes milliseconds. It doesn't lock th
          -e parent table (no impact on live queries). It doesn't generat
          -e WAL proportional to the data size. It reclaims ~500GB of dis
          -k instantly. PostgreSQL forgets the partition exists.         
      624 -                                                              
      625 -This changes the calculus significantly. You can store more in
          - Postgres than feels instinctively safe because you know the c
          -leanup is free.                                               
      626 -                                                              
      627 ----                                                           
      628 -                                                              
      629 -### The two-database pattern: when it helps, when it hurts    
      630 -                                                              
      631 -The intuition behind a Postgres + MongoDB split is: keep Postg
          -res lean (fast queries, small rows, fits in shared_buffers) an
          -d let MongoDB absorb large documents.                         
      632 -                                                              
      633 -This is correct at certain scales. It starts hurting when:    
      634 -- **Every read requires both databases.** There's no read path
          - that needs only the MongoDB data — you always need the Postgr
          -es metadata first. So every history page load becomes: Postgre
          -s query → extract refs → MongoDB batch fetch → stitch. Sequent
          -ial, two failure modes, stitching code.                       
      635 -- **The data volume doesn't justify it.** At 15GB/day, Postgre
          -s steady state is ~2.2TB over 90 days. A single r7g.2xlarge wi
          -th a 2.5TB gp3 SSD handles this. The MongoDB cluster you'd spi
          -n up to "save" Postgres would be a larger instance than the Po
          -stgres upgrade you avoided.                                   
      636 -- **You already have partitioning.** The main scaling lever fo
          -r Postgres is partition management. With monthly partitions yo
          -u're dropping 500GB per month with zero operational cost. Mong
          -oDB's TTL index is elegant, but it's solving the same problem 
          -Postgres partitioning already solves.                         
      637 -                                                              
      638 -The split becomes worthwhile when: content/day > ~30GB (templa
          -te frequency increases or sizes grow), OR when steady-state st
          -orage exceeds ~3TB and gp3 SSD costs become significant, OR wh
          -en you need cross-collection queries that MongoDB handles bett
          -er.                                                           
      639 -                                                              
      640 ----                                                           
      641 -                                                              
      642 -### How to think about each store's "job"                     
      643 -                                                              
      644 -```                                                           
      645 -PostgreSQL  =  The ledger                                     
      646 -               Durable, ordered, queryable. Answers "what happ
          -ened in this conversation?"                                   
      647 -               Optimised for: paginated access by conversation
          - + time.                                                      
      648 -                                                              
      649 -Redis       =  Working memory                                 
      650 -               Fast, ephemeral, shared. Answers "what does the
          - bot need right now?"                                         
      651 -               Optimised for: sub-ms reads, TTL expiry, atomic
          - operations.                                                  
      652 -               Not a backup for anything — data loss is surviv
          -able.                                                         
      653 -                                                              
      654 -Kafka       =  The delivery truck                             
      655 -               Ordered, durable in-transit. Bridges the SSE pa
          -th to the DB write path.                                      
      656 -               Optimised for: decoupling latency, absorbing wr
          -ite bursts, replay.                                           
      657 -                                                              
      658 -MongoDB     =  The document warehouse (not used yet)          
      659 -               Horizontal scale for large documents. Shines wh
          -en you need to store                                          
      660 -               millions of large, heterogeneous documents and 
          -access them by _id.                                           
      661 -               The right choice when Postgres JSONB storage > 
          -~3TB steady state.                                            
      662 -```                                                           
      663 -                                                              
      664 ----                                                           
      665 -                                                              
      666 -## 13. Decision Framework — When to Reconsider This Architectu
          -re                                                            
      667 -                                                              
      668 -Run through these questions when reviewing production metrics 
          -or planning capacity. The thresholds are derived from the sizi
          -ng math in Section 6.                                         
      669 -                                                              
      670 ----                                                           
      671 -                                                              
      672 -### Q1: Is total content written per day growing beyond estima
          -tes?                                                          
      673 -                                                              
      674 -**Check:** `SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('mess
          -ages'))` per partition after 30 days. Compare against the ~516
          -GB/month estimate.                                            
      675 -                                                              
      676 -| Observation | Action |                                      
      677 -|---|---|                                                     
      678 -| < 300GB/month (well below estimate) | No action. Template fr
          -equency is lower than modelled. |                             
      679 -| 300–600GB/month (within estimate) | No action. Architecture 
          -holds. |                                                      
      680 -| 600GB–1TB/month | Watch closely. Approach MongoDB split plan
          -ning but don't act yet. |                                     
      681 -| > 1TB/month (> 2× estimate) | **Trigger: initiate MongoDB sp
          -lit.** Postgres steady state will exceed 3TB within 90 days. S
          -ee Section 14. |                                              
      682 -                                                              
      683 ----                                                           
      684 -                                                              
      685 -### Q2: Are template payload sizes larger than estimated?     
      686 -                                                              
      687 -**Check:** Track `pg_column_size(content)` in the Kafka consum
          -er metrics (`size_bytes` field). Alert if p95 exceeds 120KB fo
          -r template rows.                                              
      688 -                                                              
      689 -| Observation | Action |                                      
      690 -|---|---|                                                     
      691 -| p95 < 100KB (as designed) | No action. |                    
      692 -| p95 100–200KB | Investigate which templateId is bloating. Ca
          -n the FE payload be trimmed? (e.g. return 5 images instead of 
          -20, send thumbnail URLs not full metadata). Fix the payload be
          -fore changing the DB. |                                       
      693 -| p95 > 200KB | **Trigger MongoDB split** regardless of total 
          -volume. Rows this large degrade B-tree index efficiency (TOAST
          - kicks in above 8KB; rows > ~8KB are stored off-page, requirin
          -g an extra read). |                                           
      694 -                                                              
      695 ----                                                           
      696 -                                                              
      697 -### Q3: Are history load latencies acceptable?                
      698 -                                                              
      699 -**Check:** Track `GET /api/v1/chat/get-conversation-details` p
          -95 latency. Target: < 50ms.                                   
      700 -                                                              
      701 -| Observation | Action |                                      
      702 -|---|---|                                                     
      703 -| p95 < 30ms | Healthy. |                                     
      704 -| p95 30–50ms | Check `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the messages query.
          - Ensure `(conversation_id, created_at DESC)` index is used. Ch
          -eck if shared_buffers is warm. |                              
      705 -| p95 50–150ms | Check if Postgres is doing TOAST lookups (con
          -tent > 8KB being stored off-page). Add connection headroom to 
          -PgBouncer. Consider read replica for history queries. |       
      706 -| p95 > 150ms | **Trigger: add Redis caching layer for recent 
          -history pages** (see Q5). If caching doesn't help, trigger Mon
          -goDB split. |                                                 
      707 -                                                              
      708 ----                                                           
      709 -                                                              
      710 -### Q4: Is Postgres storage becoming expensive?               
      711 -                                                              
      712 -**Check:** gp3 SSD cost at $0.08/GB. Current estimate: 2.5TB =
          - $200/month just for storage.                                 
      713 -                                                              
      714 -| Storage used | Monthly cost | Action |                      
      715 -|---|---|---|                                                 
      716 -| < 1.5TB | < $120/month | No action. |                       
      717 -| 1.5–2.5TB | $120–$200/month | Within plan. No action. |     
      718 -| 2.5–4TB | $200–$320/month | Evaluate MongoDB split at next c
          -apacity review. |                                             
      719 -| > 4TB | > $320/month | **Trigger MongoDB split.** Storage co
          -st now justifies operational complexity. |                    
      720 -                                                              
      721 ----                                                           
      722 -                                                              
      723 -### Q5: Is template frequency much lower than estimated (good 
          -news)?                                                        
      724 -                                                              
      725 -If production shows templates in < 10% of turns:              
      726 -                                                              
      727 -| Daily content | Action |                                    
      728 -|---|---|                                                     
      729 -| < 5GB/day | Switch to **quarterly partitions** (drop every 3
          - months instead of monthly). Simpler maintenance, same outcome
          -. |                                                           
      730 -| < 2GB/day | Could consolidate to a single table with a manua
          -l retention job. Partitioning overhead not worth it. |        
      731 -                                                              
      732 ----                                                           
      733 -                                                              
      734 -### Q6: Is write throughput a bottleneck?                     
      735 -                                                              
      736 -**Check:** Kafka consumer lag on `chat.messages` topic. Alert 
          -if lag > 10,000 messages.                                     
      737 -                                                              
      738 -| Observation | Action |                                      
      739 -|---|---|                                                     
      740 -| Lag < 1,000 consistently | Healthy. |                       
      741 -| Lag 1,000–10,000 | Increase batch size to 1,000 or add a 4th
          - consumer replica. |                                          
      742 -| Lag > 10,000 (sustained) | Consumer replicas maxed. Profile 
          -the bulk INSERT — likely index write overhead. Consider disabl
          -ing index maintenance during batch and rebuilding async (dange
          -rous, only with DBA). |                                       
      743 -| Writes consistently > 8,000 rows/sec | **Trigger: evaluate w
          -rite sharding** or vertical scale on Postgres primary. |      
      744 -                                                              
      745 ----                                                           
      746 -                                                              
      747 -### The decision tree (compact form)                          
      748 -                                                              
      749 -```                                                           
      750 -Is content/month > 1TB?  →  Yes → Trigger MongoDB split (Secti
          -on 14)                                                        
      751 -  ↓ No                                                        
      752 -Is p95 content row size > 200KB?  →  Yes → Trigger MongoDB spl
          -it                                                            
      753 -  ↓ No                                                        
      754 -Is history load p95 > 150ms after caching?  →  Yes → Trigger M
          -ongoDB split                                                  
      755 -  ↓ No

          - review

      759 -```

      885 --- Null out content for template rows, partition by partition

  functools.partial wires concrete implementations into abstract nodes).

  path and out_of_scope shortcut, validate_slm_node guardrail flowchart (the 3

  through summary, ADD vs REPLACE filter semantics (the first-mention-is-ADD fix

  outcomes.

  regions (the most important user-visible behaviour), sequence number

  FOLLOWUP_PROMPT_BLOCKS dispatch logic.

  (the key insight for understanding cost and correctness).

  residual vs Tier B), tool visibility matrix (what the LLM can and cannot see).

  in user. if not this user logs out then FE deletes both the login_auth_token

      31 +                                                               
      32 +### OQ-001 — Session token design                              
      33 +- **BE generates a `token_id`** on first `GET /chat/get-convers
         +ation-id` call (UUID, not JWT)                                 
      34 +- Stored as a cookie by FE, passed on every request as `token_i
         +d`                                                             
      35 +- Maps anonymous chats to a device                             
      36 +- `login-auth-token` is passed separately when user is logged i
         +n (created by Housing login service on FE; BE validates it by c
         +alling the login service API — BE does NOT create it)          
      37 +- On `migrate-chat`: `token_id` is claimed by the logged-in `us
         +er_id` → chat associated to user                               
      38 +- On logout: FE deletes both cookies. Next `get-conversation-id
         +` request → new `token_id` generated by BE                     
      39 +- **BE implementation:** simple UUID, no signing. Store mapping
         + `token_id → conversation_id` in the `conversations` table.    
      40 +                                                               
      41 +### OQ-002 — contactSeller                                     
      42 +- **BE never calls Venus CRM or any seller API**               
      43 +- BE identifies the `contact_seller` intent → sends `contact_se
         +ller` template to FE with `property_id`                        
      44 +- **FE calls its own APIs** to get seller details and show them
         + to the user                                                   
      45 +- This means: `execute_tier1_action` for `contact_seller` just 
         +returns a template payload, nothing else                       
      46 +- Venus CRM, seller APIs, lead creation = entirely FE responsib
         +ility                                                          
      47 +- **Impact on CHAT-P-030**: remove Venus/CRM integration; `cont
         +act_seller` Tier 1 = emit template only                        
      48 +                                                               
      49 +### OQ-003 — Anonymous users + portfolio                       
      50 +- `portfolio/recent_searches`: **works with `token_id`** — BE s
         +tores search history keyed by token_id, no login required      
      51 +- All other portfolio intents (`saved_properties`, `viewed_prop
         +erties`, `recommendations`): **hard login block** → `login` tem
         +plate                                                          
      52 +- **Impact on CHAT-A-008**: session must track `search_history`
         + keyed by `token_id` (even for anonymous)                      
      53 +                                                               
      54 +### OQ-004 — transaction_type inference                        
      55 +- **Message + conversation context only** — user's profile is N
         +OT consulted                                                   
      56 +- SLM infers buy/rent from message signals ("under 80L" → buy, 
         +"2500/month" → rent)                                           
      57 +- Session holds `transaction_type` once inferred; SLM can updat
         +e it on a pivot                                                
      58 +- No profile API call needed                                   
      59 +

      212 -`GET /api/v1/chat/get-conversation-id` — creates or returns ex
          -isting conversation.                                          
      213 -See `docs/api/endpoints.md` Part A1.                          
      212 +`GET /api/v1/chat/get-conversation-id` — the entry point for e
          +very session.                                                 
      213 +Also the source of the `token_id` (BE-generated device identif
          +ier for anonymous users).                                     
      214  
      215 +**Session token design (PM-confirmed):**                      
      216 +```                                                           
      217 +Anonymous flow:                                               
      218 +  1. FE calls GET /chat/get-conversation-id (no headers)      
      219 +  2. BE generates token_id = UUID4, creates conversation row  
      220 +  3. BE returns { conversationId, tokenId, isNew: true }      
      221 +  4. FE stores tokenId in cookie, sends on every future reques
          +t as X-Token-ID header                                        
      222 +                                                              
      223 +Logged-in flow:                                               
      224 +  1. FE calls GET /chat/get-conversation-id with Login-Auth-To
          +ken header                                                    
      225 +  2. BE calls login service API to validate the token → gets u
          +ser_id                                                        
      226 +  3. BE looks up existing conversation for this user_id, or cr
          +eates new one                                                 
      227 +  4. Returns { conversationId, isNew } (no tokenId in response
          + — FE already has it)                                         
      228 +                                                              
      229 +migrate-chat:                                                 
      230 +  1. User logs in while in an anonymous chat                  
      231 +  2. FE calls POST /chat/migrate-chat with Login-Auth-Token + 
          +currentConversationId                                         
      232 +  3. BE validates login token → gets user_id                  
      233 +  4. Updates conversations SET user_id = ? WHERE conversation_
          +id = ? AND token_id = ?                                       
      234 +  5. Chat is now owned by the logged-in user                  
      235 +```                                                           
      236 +                                                              
      237 +**Login service API call:**                                   
      238 +```python                                                     
      239 +async def validate_login_token(login_auth_token: str) -> str |
          + None:                                                        
      240 +    """Calls Housing login service to validate token. Returns 
          +user_id or None."""                                           
      241 +    resp = await http_client.get(                             
      242 +        f"{settings.login_service_url}/validate",             
      243 +        headers={"Login-Auth-Token": login_auth_token},       
      244 +    )                                                         
      245 +    if resp.status_code == 200:                               
      246 +        return resp.json()["userId"]                          
      247 +    return None                                               
      248 +```                                                           
      249 +                                                              
      250 +Add `LOGIN_SERVICE_URL` to `.env.example`.                    
      251 +                                                              
      252  **Acceptance Criteria:**
      216 -- [ ] Logged-in user: returns existing conversation for `login
          --auth-token` or creates new one                               
      217 -- [ ] Anonymous: returns existing conversation for `tokenId` c
          -ookie or creates new one                                      
      218 -- [ ] Response shape: `{"conversationId": "uuid", "isNew": tru
          -e}`                                                           
      219 -- [ ] Creates `conversations` row in PostgreSQL (via Kafka ses
          -sion_events, not synchronous)                                 
      220 -- [ ] Session initialized in Redis with empty state           
      253 +- [ ] Anonymous: generates `token_id` (UUID4), stores in `conv
          +ersations.token_id`                                           
      254 +- [ ] Response: `{"conversationId": "uuid", "tokenId": "uuid",
          + "isNew": true}`                                              
      255 +- [ ] Logged-in: validates `Login-Auth-Token` via login servic
          +e; maps to `user_id`                                          
      256 +- [ ] If login service is down: fall back to anonymous flow (l
          +og warning)                                                   
      257 +- [ ] Session initialized in Redis with empty state on convers
          +ation creation                                                
      258 +- [ ] `conversations` row created via Kafka `chat.session_even
          +ts` (not synchronous)

⏺ 12 documents, ~2,381 lines total. Here's the full summary of what was
  clarified and updated:

  ---
  What changed based on PM clarifications

  Session token (OQ-001) — simpler than designed

  token_id is a plain UUID4 generated by BE. No JWT, no signing. Stored in
  cookie by FE, passed on every request. When the user logs in, FE passes
  login-auth-token (from Housing login service) instead — BE validates it via a
  login service API call, NOT by generating anything. migrate-chat claims the
  token_id for the logged-in user_id. On logout, FE deletes both cookies; next
  request gets a fresh token_id. CHAT-A-007 SP reduced from 2→3 (login service
  API validation added) but complexity is actually lower.

  contactSeller (OQ-002) — BE does zero CRM work

  BE identifies the intent, emits contact_seller template with property_id. FE
  calls its own APIs to get seller details and handle the contact flow.
  CHAT-P-030 SP reduced from 5→3 — no Venus/CRM integration needed from BE at
  all.

  Portfolio auth (OQ-003) — split by intent

  recent_searches works with token_id (no login required — stored in session
  keyed by device token). Everything else (saved_properties, viewed_properties,
  recommendations) → hard login block → login template. Updated INTENT_REGISTRY
  note: recent_searches.requires_auth = False.

  transaction_type (OQ-004) — pure conversation context

  No profile API call. SLM infers from message context only. Simplifies the
  session initialization flow.

  experiments.yaml (OQ-005) — git-tracked

  Committed to repo. No credentials in this file. If an experiment needs
  credentials or sensitive targeting → feature flag service. For MVP: all
  experiments in config/experiments.yaml.

  ---
  Dry run mode — the new capability

  Four new tickets (DRY-001 through DRY-004):

  1. DryRunExecutor (@priya, Sprint 1): fixture-based CachedExecutorPort that
  reads from tests/fixtures/scenarios/. Records all tool calls for assertions.
  Raises ToolFixtureMissing with helpful message when a fixture isn't found.
  2. 10 scenario files (@rahul, Sprint 1): QA authors JSON fixtures for every
  key intent flow — plausible Mumbai property data, real locality names,
  realistic prices. Covers: 2BHK search, property detail, locality research,
  comparison, portfolio, clarification, Hindi ordinal, out_of_scope.
  3. make dry-run CLI (@arjun, Sprint 1): BOT_ENV=mock DRY_RUN_SCENARIO=X
  auto-wires the dry run executor. make dry-run SCENARIO=2bhk_bandra_search 
  MSG="show me 2bhk in bandra" runs the full pipeline in ~2s, prints all SSE
  events with classification result and timing.
  4. Intent identification test suite (@rahul, Sprint 2): pytest suite that runs
  each scenario and asserts on main_intent, sub_intent, templateId, and SSE
  event sequence. Runs in < 60s on any machine with only ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set.
  No VPN needed.

  The key unlock: AI engineers can develop and test any pipeline node change by
  running make dry-run in under 5 seconds, on any machine, without VPN or a
  running chat-demo. The dry run is not a mock of the LLM/SLM (those are still
  real Anthropic calls) — it mocks only the data-fetching tool executors. This
  means intent classification quality, session state, SSE event ordering, and
  node logic are all validated against real AI calls.

  ---
  The dry run philosophy (the new insight)

  The dry run is not a CLI convenience. It is the primary integration testing 
  harness — the layer where requirements become verifiable. Here's why this
  matters:

  Without dry run: unit test passes → merge → real API has different shape →
                   E2E fails → debug session → fix → re-test → 2-day loop

  With dry run:    unit test passes → dry run test passes with fixture →
                   merge → integration test validates real API shape (once per
  sprint) →
                   30-minute loop

  The InMemorySessionStore + DryRunExecutor + run_dry_pipeline() function means
  @priya can implement filter_apply_node, run make dry-run 
  SCENARIO=2bhk_bandra_search MSG="show me 2bhk in bandra under 80L", and see
  the full pipeline output — classification, SSE events in order, session
  mutation, filter_delta applied — in under 5 seconds, on any machine, without
  VPN.

  @rahul starts writing tests against run_dry_pipeline() in Sprint 1, before any
  real API integration exists. The scenario fixtures ARE the spec — when real
  APIs disagree with fixtures, the fixtures win (contract-first).
